Durgāsūkta
(‘hymn in praise of दुर्गा’)
------------------------------------------
This is a short, but well-known and popular Vedic सूक्त. There are only seven mantras. These mantras, though forming a part of the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (

), are spread over in the Ṛgveda, the Taittirīya Saṁhitā and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.
Out of the seven mantras only the second concerns दुर्गा. The seventh is a prayer addressed to इन्द्र. The other five are related to अग्नि. Yet, tradition has considered all the mantras as one unit and called them Durgāsūkta.
Its recitation is specially recommended for overcoming the difficulties in life. It is believed that दुर्गा (the Divine मोथेर्) and अग्नि (the deity of fire) protect us from internal and external enemies.
The following is a brief summary of the hymn:
May we extract the सोम juice in order to offer as oblation to Jātavedas, अग्नि who is all knowing. May he destroy our enemies. May he take us across all perils even as a ship takes us across the sea. May he also protect us from all wrongs.
I take refuge in her, the goddess दुर्गा, who is lustrous like fire, who is radiating power through her तपस् (austerity), who belongs to Paramātmā or the Supreme God and who is worshipped by the votaries through various rites to get their fruits. Our salutations to you who is skilled in taking us across the ocean of सṁसार.
O अग्नि! You are worthy of praise. Through auspicious means take us beyond all difficulties, to the other shore. May our home-town and home-land become extensive and may the plot of agricultural land also be ample. Further, may you be pleased to bless our children and grandchildren with joy.
O अग्नि! You destroy all our sins and take us beyond all troubles. You protect us just as one who takes a person across the sea by a ship. O Fire-god! Guard our bodies and be mindful of its safety like the sage अत्रि who always prayed mentally (for the good of all).
We invoke from the highest place of assembly, अग्नि (the Fire-god) who is the conqueror of enemies, the charger of foes, and who is fierce. May he, the Fire-god, take us across all our difficulties and wrongs, and all that is perishable, and protect us.
You are lauded in sacrifices. You increase our happiness. You are seated in the sacrificial place as ancient and modern sacrificer. O अग्नि, be pleased to make us happy, we who are your own selves. Grant us good fortune from all sides.
O इन्द्र! You are unconnected (with sin and sorrow). You pervade (all sacrifices). (Desirous of good fortune) comprising cattle and overflowing (with the current of immortal bliss), may we serve you. May the gods who dwell in the highest region of हेअवेन् delight me—practising loving adoration of Viṣṇu—here on earth by granting my wish.
In some of the readings, a गायत्री-मन्त्र of दुर्गा is added thus:
kātyāyanāya vidmahe । kanyakumāri dhīmahi । tanno durgiḥ pracodayāt ॥
Its meaning is: We know कात्यायनी (daughter of the sage Katyāyana). We meditate upon Kanyākumāri! May she, दुर्गा, impel our understanding in the right direction!

Durvāsas
(‘[One who is] difficult to live with’)
------------------------------------------
If there was one sage in the entire mythological literature of हिन्दुइस्म् who was the very embodiment of anger and the propensity for cursing, it was दुर्वासस्. For this very nature of his, he was a difficult (= dur) man to live with (= vāsa). However, when pleased, he was capable of bestowing great boons too.
He was the third son of the sage अत्रि and his wife अनसूया, the paragon of wifely virtues, born as a partial इन्चर्नतिओन् of शिव.
He is sometimes described as the human personification of शिव’s arrow that destroyed Tripuras or the Three cities of the demons who were the sons of तारकासुर.
His exploits and feats range from the sublime to the not-so-sublime levels. They can be summarised as follows:
Pleased with the maiden कुन्ती, the daughter of the king Kuntibhoja, for her devoted service, he gave her a मन्त्र with the help of which she could invite any deity and get a son from his grace. The five Pāṇḍavas and कर्ण were born by the power of this मन्त्र.
As per his direction, कृष्ण smeared his body (except the feet) with the remnants of the pāyasa (pudding) eaten by the sage. This made his body (except the soles of his feet) invulnerable to weapons.
He completed the half-done sacrifice of the king Śvetaki and enabled him to ascend to हेअवेन्.
He tried to harm the Pāṇḍavas (when they were in the forest) at the behest of दुर्योधन but was made to flee by the divine intervention of कृष्ण.
His unjustified anger against the virtuous king अम्बरीष created a real crisis in his own life. He had to run for cover, being relentlessly pursued by the सुदर्शन-चक्र (the discus-weapon of Lord विष्णु). He was ultimately rescued by the king himself!
He was responsible for the banishment and subsequent demise of लक्ष्मण by forcing him to go against राम’s command.

dūrvā
(‘that which destroys [sin]’)
------------------------------------------
Dūrvā (Cynodon dactylon), a common variety of grass found all over India, has been considered as sacred and fit to be used in worship and other religious rites. After taking bath in a river or a tank, a little of this grass, with a small quantity of mud is placed on the head and some mantras (vide Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1.34 and 35) are repeated as an act of purification. In these mantras दूर्वा has been praised as a deity.
When दूर्वा grows tall, it is called ‘darbha’. Rings made of दर्भ are tied to the ring-finger at the commencement of many a religious rite. It is then called ‘pavitra’, ‘that which ‘sanctifies’.
Dūrvā, considered as dear to the deity गणपति, is extensively used in his worship.
The works on आयुर्वेद sometimes mention three varieties of दूर्वा: nīladūrvā, śvetadūrvā, and gaṇḍadūrvā. Several medicinal properties are attributed to them. As such it is an appetiser, an analgesic, a purifier of blood, a remedy for skin troubles and a cure for diarrhoea.

Durgā Temple
(of ऐहोऌए)
------------------------------------------
One of the more ancient group of temples, built out of stone and preserved as archaeological monuments is at ऐहोऌए, a small town in the Bijapur district of northern Karnataka. The दुर्गा तेम्प्ले is a major building of this group. The temple derives its name because it is situated inside a structure that resembles a ‘durga’ or fort and not because it is dedicated to the goddess दुर्गा. It is assigned to the period A.

and is of the Cāḷukyan style. The apsidal plinth resembles Buddhist चैत्य in architectural style. The विमान (tower above the main shrine) is of the नागर type. (See NĀGARA for details.)
There is no image of any deity inside the sanctum. There is a passage round it meant for pradakṣiṇā or circumambulation.
The pillars carrying the roof are rectangular in shape and are of a very simple design. The relief figures etched on the outer walls and on the pillars in the front include: Rāmā and सीता seated in a boat navigated by गुह, शिव riding his bull (Nandi), विष्णु, नरसिṁह, Varāha, दुर्गा, गरुड, Gaṇgā and यमुना.
There is reason to believe that it was a Vaiṣṇava temple.
The stone inscriptions discovered here do not give any significant details or information about the temple and its builders.
See also AIHOḶE.

Durgāṣṭamī-vrata
(‘the religious vows to be observed on the eighth day [devoted to the worship of the] goddess दुर्गा’)
------------------------------------------
Vratas and utsavas (religious vows and celebrations) are an important aspect of popular हिन्दुइस्म्.
The Devīpurāṇa, a minor work, refers to a दुर्गाष्टमी-व्रत, which has no reference to the exploits of the goddess दुर्गा like the killing of महिषासुर. It is entirely different from the दुर्गापूजा or दुर्गोत्सव.
It is observed on the śukla aṣṭamī days only, for one year, beginning from Śrāvaṇa-śukla-aṣṭamī (the eighth day in the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, usually in July/August). Feeding of virgins and ब्राह्मणस्, apart from a worship of दुर्गा, is an important item of this vrata.

Durgāsaptaśatī
(‘seven hundred [verses on] दुर्गा’)
------------------------------------------
See DEVĪMĀHĀTMYA.

Durgāpūjā
(‘worship of दुर्गा’, ‘festival of दुर्गा’)
------------------------------------------
The worship of God as शक्ति (Supreme Power) and as देवी (Divine मोथेर्, मोथेर् of the Universe) is as old as the Ṛgveda itself. Over the centuries it has grown into a formidable cult with its own philosophy, myths and rituals. The दुर्गापूजा is undoubtedly the most important festival of this religious tradition.
Durgāpūjā ProcessionAs in the case of many other important व्रतस् अन्द् उत्सवस्, the दुर्गोत्सव is both नित्य (compulsory) and kāmya (optional). It may be performed for nine days or just three days (from Āśvayuja śukla saptamī to navamī ). Those who want to celebrate it just for a day, can do so either on the aṣṭamī or on the navamī day.
It is interesting to note that the various gods of the Hindu pantheon, including विष्णु, are described as going to sleep for a period of four months (Āṣāḍha to Kārttīka). That the rainy season spread over this four-month period gave little scope to movement and activity or that the sun gave very little light to the Vedic आर्यन्स् living the northern latitudes, may have been the origin of this myth.
Be that as it may, since मोथेर् दुर्गा who goes to bed on आषाढ śukla aṣṭamī, is still sleeping at the time the दुर्गोत्सव is planned to be celebrated, she has to be woken up first! This is called ‘bodhana’ and is done on the evening of Āśvayuja śukla षष्ठी. A घट or कलश (a pot with water containing sandalwood paste, दूर्वा grass, leaves of five trees like mango, clay from seven places, fruit etc.) is established under a बिल्व tree (Aegle marmelos), the mantras of बोधन or awakening are uttered, and the बिल्व tree itself is worshipped as मोथेर् दुर्गा. A second घट is also established there itself. Next morning (i.e., on the saptamī day), a small branch of that बिल्व tree is cut, placed in the second घट and ceremonially carried to the hall of worship where the clay image has already been established, and kept at its feet. After प्राणप्रतिष्ठा, a detailed worship is done to the घट (in the presence of the image) with sixteen उपचारस्, followed by होम (sacrifice in a duly consecrated fire).
The story goes that when दुर्गा (or पार्वती ) came to her मोथेर्’s होउसे from her husband’s home, it was late evening. So, she decided not to disturb her parents and spent the whole night under a बिल्व tree near the होउसे. The ritual described above is symbolic of this.
Durgāpūjā idol immersionThe pūjās done on the aṣṭamī and navamī days are practically identical with the saptamī पूजा. On all the days, स्नान or bath is given to the sword or the mirror kept in front of the image reflecting it. Again, on all the days, ceremonial recitation of the famous work Devīmāhātmya (also known as Śrī Caṇḍī and Durgā-saptaśatī ) is arranged at a suitable place in the worship hall. This recitation, especially on such holy days, is considered to confer great benefits on the performer of the पूजा.
Part of the aśṭamī पूजा is the Kumarīpūjā, worship of a girl-child in the age-group of 2 to 10. She should be a healthy child unblemished in body and appearance. She is to be worshipped as the embodiment of the देवी or goddess herself.
Another important ritual is the Sandhipūjā, performed at the junction of the two tithis, aṣṭamī and navamī. The देवी along with the योगिनीस् (various emanations of the देवी, 64 in all) is to be worshipped then. A बलि (sacrifice) is also to be given.
Though animal sacrifice has existed as part of दुर्गापूजा, it is relegated as tāmasic (bad or evil), fit for people of lower culture and evolution.
On the early morning of daśamī, the tenth day, the visarjanapūjā (worship signifying a send-off to the goddess) is done, symbolically withdrawing the deity from the image into one’s own heart. In the evening, after a simple ārati (waving of light) the image is taken in a grand procession and immersed in a tank or a river or the sea. Much revelry is seen during the procession and afterwards, in the manner of the festivities of Śabaras (mountain tribes or barbarian tribes). In this शबरोत्सव, as it is called, all people irrespective of their social status, were expected to join, probably emphasizing that all were equal before the मोथेर् of all.
The evening of विजयदशमी, after the immersion of the दुर्गा image, is an occasion of great joy for the people who meet their friends and relatives and warmly greet them.
The दुर्गोत्सव described till now as the biggest festival, is mainly celebrated in Bengal, Bihar and Assam. However, now-a-days, it is being celebrated in the urban areas of almost all parts of the country, thanks to the concentration of the Bengali population there.
See also DURGĀ.

Durgā
(‘the One [who is] difficult [to approach]’)
------------------------------------------
Durgā is, perhaps the most widely worshipped aspect of शक्ति. An entire Purāna, the Devībhāgavata, has been dedicated to her. Another work, more well-known than the Devībhāgavata, but containing practically the same material in a concise from, is the Devīmāhātmyam. It is also known as the Durgāsaptaśatī or Caṇḍī, and forms a part of another well-known purāṇa, the Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa. This work is so highly venerated that every verse of it is considered to be a मन्त्र (sacred formula) of the देवी and its repetition is believed to confer whatever boons the votary prays for.
Literally ‘Durgā’ means one who is difficult to approach, or, difficult to know. Being the personification of the totality of the powers of the gods, she is naturally difficult to approach or to know. However, being the मोथेर् of the universe, she is the personification of tender love, when supplicated.
Out of the several aspects of the शक्ति put forward by this work, योगनिद्रा (‘meditation-sleep’) comes first. She is the power of sleep, taking recourse to which, Lord विष्णु rests between two cycles of च्रेअतिओन्. She is praised as responsible for the च्रेअतिओन्, sustenance and withdrawal of the universe. She is the mysterious power, the very personification of know-ledge, wisdom and memory. She is pleasant and beautiful. At the same time she is terrible also. This combination of the opposite qualities is possible only for her. She is described as wielding several weapons like the bow, arrow, sword, discus and trident.
The next is Mahiṣāsuramardinī, the deity who took shape as a result of the pooling together of the powers of all the gods, who had been oppressed by the demon महिषासुर. विष्णु, शिव and ब्रह्मा were incensed by hearing the accounts of the misdeeds of महिषासुर and the देवी was born out of their wrath, followed by the wrath of the lesser divinities. The powers of these gods formed her limbs and the exact duplicates of their weapons formed her arsenal. Armed with these formidable weapons and riding on a fierce lion, she challenged महिषासुर and destroyed him along with his army.
This story is followed by an exquisite hymn which combines in itself both poetic excellence and devotional fervour and insight. She is the power inscrutable, by which the whole universe is permeated and energised. She is the personification of all wealth, power, beauty, as also virtues. She is the embodiment of यज्ञ (sacrifice), parāvidyā (the highest know-ledge concerning the spirit) as well as aparāvidyā (knowledge of the secular sciences). It is she who bestows wealth—both material and spiritual—dispels difficulties, and annihilates the evil ones. Her beauty as well as her valour, is incomparable.
The gods could not enjoy their freedom for long. Very soon, they were overpowered by the demons Śumbha and Niśumbha. So they had to run to the हिमालयस् and supplicate the देवी again. This hymn, well-known as the ‘Aparājitā-स्तोत्र,’ praises her as the ‘unconquered’. Her immanence in all the living beings is the main theme of this hymn. The powers and activities of all beings are manifestations of only her power.
In response to this prayer, she manifested herself as Kauśikī दुर्गा, emanating from the body of पार्वती, who herself became Kālī the dark one, after this manifestation.
The world-bewitching beauty of दुर्गा attracted the attention of Śumbha and Niśumbha who sent proposals of मर्रिअगे through a serf. Unfortunately for them, in a moment of ‘weakness and foolishness’ she had vowed to marry only him who would vanquish her in battle. All attempts at forcibly dragging her away ended in disaster for the demons. Heads rolled, the intervention of giants like Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa, मुण्ड and Rakta-बीज not withstanding. Kālī, the fierce black goddess who emerged from the देवी’s forehead, beheaded Caṇḍa and मुण्ड and thus won the name चामुण्डा for herself. Only the battle with Raktabīja was longdrawn needing some special efforts by the देवी since he had the mysterious power to multiply himself through the drops of blood spilled in the battle. Even the सप्तमातृकास् (seven Mothers) who came out of her body to battle, seemed helpless. It was Kālī who managed to spread her extensive tongue and drink away all the blood gushing out of Raktabīja, thus preventing the emergence of more demons and enabling दुर्गा to exterminate him. The rest was easy. Niśumbha was easily put to death after a mockery of fight. Śumbha being exasperated by now, accused her of taking the help of ‘others!’ Laughing derisively, the देवी withdrew all her emanations and manifestations into herself, showing that she was always the One without a second. In the ensuing battle, Śumbha the lord of the demons, was easily killed, thus ridding the worlds of the great terror.
This is followed by another piece of prayer, an enchanting poetical hymn, which is as simple as it is elegant. Known as the ‘Nārāyaṇīstuti’ it starts with a fervent appeal to the मोथेर् by the grateful gods to be benign and gracious. The hymn describes her as the mistress and the मोथेर् of the whole च्रेअतिओन्. She is the physical universe. She is the mysterious power of विष्णु (Vaiṣṇavīśakti), the original cause, as also the power that deludes beings. It is only by pleasing her that one can hope to get spiritual emanci-pation. All arts and sciences as also womankind, are her manifestations. She is residing as the intellect in the hearts of human beings. She is the all-devouring time. She is the very personification of all that is good and auspicious. She is ever engaged in protecting her children. The सप्तमातृकास् are really her aspects. Kālī the terrible, with a garland of human skulls round her neck, is also another of her aspects. When pleased, she can remedy all diseases. If displeased, she can destroy all that we love and like to possess. Her votaries are always free from troubles. She is the Supreme Truth described in all the scriptural works.
The work also describes her other manifestations like Vindhyavāsinī (one who lives in the Vindhyas), Raktadantā (of red teeth), Śatākṣī (of hundred eyes), Śākaṁbharī (sustainer of vegetables), दुर्गा (slayer of demon Durgama), Bhīmā (the terrible) and Bhrāmarī or भ्रम-rāmbā (having the form of bees).
The देवी as depicted in this work has three major manifestations: Mahākālī, महालक्ष्मी and Mahāsarasvatī. These aspects should not be confused with the pauraṇic deities, पार्वती, लक्ष्मी and सरस्वती. They are actually the three major manifestations of the One Supreme Power Maheśvarī, according to the three guṇas (tamas, रजस् and सत्त्व).
The first, Mahākalī, has ten faces and ten feet. She is deep blue in colour, like the gem Nīlamaṇi. She is bedecked with ornaments and wields in her ten hands, the following weapons and objects: sword, discus, mace, arrow, bow, iron club, lance, sling, human head and conch. Being the personification of the tāmasic aspect of the देवी, she is also the योगनिद्रा, who has put Lord विष्णु to sleep. It is to her that ब्रह्मा prayed, requesting her to leave विष्णु so that the latter could destroy the demons मधु and कैटभ.
She is the personification of Māyā, the mysterious power of Lord विष्णु. Unless she is pleased and voluntarily withdraws, the Lord in us will not awake and destroy the powers of evil which are trying to destroy us. This seems to be the import of the story of ब्रह्मा, मधु and कैटभ.
Mahālakṣmī, the second, the rājasic aspect of the देवी is described as red in colour like the coral. She holds in her eighteen hands the rosary, battle-pot, cudgel, lance, sword, shield, conch, bell, wine-cup, trident, noose and the discus सुदर्शन. Being ‘born’ out of the combined wraths and powers of all the gods, she is the personification not only of the powers but also of the will to fight the evil forces. That is why she is shown as red in colour, the colour of blood, the colour of war. It is she who destroyed महिषासुर.
The story of महिषासुर has several implications. महिषासुर, the he-buffalo, represents the jungle law that might is right. He is the ruthless brute force that does not brook any opposition where selfish ends are concerned. And he succeeded even against the gods; but only when they were divided. But he fell before their combined powers and the will to fight, which is exactly what the देवी, महिषासुर-mardinī, represents. The lesson of this story at the social level is too obvious to need an explanation. Nor can we ignore its social implications. At the subjective level, महिषासुर stands for इग्नोरन्चे and stubborn egoism. Its subju-gation and conquest are possible only when the sādhaka (spiritual aspirant) pools all his energies together and fights it with a tenacious will. Since God helps him who helps himself, the intervention of the divine power in his favour is always there.
Mahāsarasvatī is the third deity representing the sāttvic aspect of the देवी. She is bright like the autumn मोओन् and has eight hands in which she holds the bell, trident, ploughshare, conch, pestle, discus, bow and arrow. It is she who manifests out of the physical sheath of पार्वती and hence known as Kauśikī दुर्गा. She is the very personification of physical perfection and beauty. She is the power of work, order and organization.
The section dealing with her exploits is the longest. Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa, मुण्ड, Raktabīja, Niśumbha and Śumbha are the chief demons destroyed by her. All these demons known as असुरस्, are archetypes of highly egoistic people who revel in a life of the pleasures of the body and the sense-organs. Symbolically they represent various stages and states of egoism. If Dhūmralocana (‘the smoky-eyed’) stands for the grossest state of इग्नोरन्चे and egoism, Raktabīja represents a more subtle state which multiplies itself and our troubles! While मुण्ड is the low profile of our egoism (muṇḍa = the low), Caṇḍa is the more horrible side of it (caṇḍa = fierce). Śumbha and Niśumbha signify more englightened aspects of egoism (Śumbh = to shine).
Dhūmralocana was destroyed by a huṅkāra, by a mere frown! Caṇḍa and मुण्ड were too mean to be handled by the देवी directly. Hence Kālī, the horrible, finished them at her behest. Raktabīja required more skilful handling. The source of his strength was destroyed first before destroying him. As for Niśumbha and Śumbha, the देवी was obliged to give them a straight fight. Lower states of इग्नोरन्चे and egoism as typified by Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa and मुण्ड, should be destroyed by sudden bursts of energy and rough handling. More crafty states which result in endless multiplication of desires—that is what Raktabīja signifies—should be tactfully handled by going to the root, by suppressing them as soon as they arise. ‘Enlightened egoism,’ if one can use such an expression, which is egoism all the same, needs a straight fight. It may be a long drawn fight and देवी’s grace is absolutely necessary for success.
Aspects of दुर्गा mentioned in the पुराणस् and आगमस् are legion. For instance: Śailaputrī, Kūṣmāṇḍā, Kātyā-yanī, क्षेमङ्करी, Harasiddhiḥ, Vana-दुर्गा, Vindhyavāsinī, Jayadurgā and so on. They are of greater interest in icono-graphy and to the supplicants who can get different types of desires fulfilled by worshipping the different aspects.
Images of दुर्गा can have four or eight or ten or eighteen or even twenty hands. The eyes are usually three. The hair is dressed up as a crown (called करण्ड-मुकुट). She is gorgeously dressed with red cloth and several ornaments. Among the objects held in hand, the more common ones are—conch, discus, trident, bow, arrow, sword, dagger, shield, rosary, winecup and bell. She may be shown as standing on a lotus or on a buffalo’s head or as riding a lion.
Lion, the royal beast, her mount, represents the best in animal च्रेअतिओन्. It can also represent the greed for ड़ोओद् and hence the greed for other objects of enjoyment which inevitably leads to lust. To become divine (devatva) one should keep one’s animal instincts under complete control. This seems to be the lesson we can draw from the picture of Siṁha-vāhinī (the rider of lion).

dūrohaṇa
------------------------------------------
In yajñas and yāgas (sacrifices), Vedic mantras are invariably recited. There are specific rules guiding their recitation. These include not only the modes of intonation but also of repetition. One such is the दूरोहण method mentioned by the commentary (of Devasvāmin) on the Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtras (

and 13). According to this mode, while chanting a मन्त्र the following should be the order:
ascending order : First pāda, half verse and then three pādas at a stretch, followed by a pause.
descending order : Three pādas, half verse, pāda and then the entire verse without a pause.

Duryodhana
------------------------------------------
It was the villainy of दुर्योधन (also known as Suyodhana), the personification of greed and jealousy, and the inordinate attachment of धृतराष्ट्र, his blind ड़थेर्, that led to the tragic war of कुरुक्षेत्र, resulting in the total extirpation of the Kaurava race.
At the time of his birth there were numerous ill-omens that made many a sane well-wisher of the कुरु-Pāṇḍava race, exhort धृतराष्ट्र to abandon this evil boy. But the blind infatuation of this sightless ड़थेर् made him to ignore their wise counsels, ultimately leading to disastrous consequences.
The Kaurava and the Pāṇḍava princes underwent their training and एदुचतिओन्, first under Kṛpācārya and then under द्रोणाचार्य. The brilliance and the remarkable progress of the Pāṇḍavas roused the envy and the hatred of दुर्योधन to such an extent that he tried his best to eliminate them by abominable means such as poisoning and arson. But none of his tricks worked, thanks to the timely intervention of विदुर and other well-wishers of the Pāṇḍavas.
When the Pāṇḍavas along with their newly wed wife द्रौपदी, were given half the kingdom and they started ruling from their capital इन्द्रप्रस्थ, their popularity and prosperity further fuelled his fire of jealousy. He invited युधिष्ठिर for गम्ब्लिन्ग् through a game of dice. Since the latter had a great weakness for it he readily consented, but was easily vanquished by the crafty शकुनि, the uncle of दुर्योधन, who had substituted for him. The result was an utter debacle for the Pāṇḍavas who lost everything. Taking this as an opportunity, दुश्शासन, the second of the Kauravas tried to molest and disrobe the Pāṇḍava queen Draupaḍī, whose honour was saved by the divine intervention of Śrī कृष्ण. धृतराष्ट्र then gave them back their kingdom and they returned to इन्द्रप्रस्थ.
Duryodhana contrived with शकुनि to have a second round of the game of dice with युधिष्ठिर. The latter lost in it his kingdom and was banished for a period of thirteen years. The first twelve years were to be spent in a forest and the last year incognito. If found out during that period, they had to repeat it all over, once again. दुर्योधन tried hard to find them out and mounted an attack against them, then living in the capital of the king विराट. But, he tasted a humiliating defeat. By this time, the Pāṇḍavas had completed their thirteenth year too.
When they demanded their kingdom back, दुर्योधन flatly refused, saying that he would not yield even as much land as would be covered by the point of a needle. कृष्ण’s last ditch efforts too, for peace, failed. दुर्योधन’s attempt to capture and imprison कृष्ण was nullified by the latter’s yogic powers.
In the ensuing war, दुर्योधन lost his all and ultimately died in a duel with भीम.
